title: Role-based access control
idea: Role-based access control (RBAC) decides what a user may do from the role they hold, not from who they are.

analogy.text: Hotel key cards are either guest or staff. Each door checks the card type, not the holder's name.
analogy.breaks: Nothing guards a door until your code adds the check.

points: A permission is one allowed action, such as `books:write`.
A role is a named bundle of permissions. This book uses `user` and `admin`.
A user holds a role, so editing the role updates every holder.
A request passes when the caller's role holds the needed permission; otherwise `403`.

steps.caption: Ada holds the `user` role. Grace holds the `admin` role.
Permissions attach to roles, never to people. Follow the arrows from each role.
Ada reads books. Her role holds `books:read`, so the request passes.
Ada lists users. Her role has no path to `users:read`, so she gets `403`.
Grace lists users. `admin` holds `users:read`, so she passes.

code.title: Roles and permissions
code.caption: Run it. Then add `'books:write'` to `user` and see which line changes.

pitfalls: Avoid one role per person. A role describes a job, not an individual.
Start new users on the lowest role and promote them on purpose.
Deny when the role is unknown or missing; never allow by default.

quiz.why: Permissions belong to the role, so adding `write` to `user` changes every user. A role nobody defined gets nothing.

takeaway: Give permissions to roles, roles to users, and check on the server.

starters: What is the difference between a role and a permission?
Can one user hold several roles?
How do I let users edit only their own records?
